# R9 — Justification

Every semantic unit of `library/core/rules/R9-scope-is-budget.md`, why it exists, what fails without it, and where it comes from. Sources are the nine repositories in `SOURCES.md` and the blueprint sections named by ID.

| # | Unit | Why it exists | What breaks if removed | Source / inspiration |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Title and ID `R9 — Scope is budget` | The ID is the handle other documents cite; the title is the whole rule in four words. | Other parts cite an unnamed rule; a title like "avoid scope creep" names a symptom, not the mechanism (a budget that can be spent). | Blueprint R9 |
| 2 | "paid for in time, code, content, tests, and upkeep" | Names the five currencies so a cost estimate has fields, not a feeling. | Cost collapses to "a few days"; the upkeep after release — the expensive part — is never counted. | OpenMW: "maintaining features comes at a cost and our resources are limited"; OpenTTD "scope and goals" |
| 3 | "upkeep that outlives it" | The reason a shipped feature keeps costing: compatibility, migrations, regressions. | Features look free once built; the budget is checked only before the work, never after. | OpenMW feature policy; Homebrew "remain practical for Homebrew to support" |
| 4 | "Scope is a number you spend, not a list you lengthen" | Replaces the wish-list mental model with a spendable quantity. | Scope is read as a checklist; adding a line feels neutral because nothing is decremented. | Blueprint R9; OpenTTD one-year horizon |
| 5 | Why: "A game stops shipping when each idea looks cheap alone" | States the failure mode the rule prevents, in one line. | The rule reads as bureaucracy and is skipped exactly when the developer is most excited. | OpenMW feature policy; k8s Enhancements Freeze |
| 6 | Examples: "A word list, an extra enemy, a mode" | Three sizes of the same mistake, so the rule is not read as "no new systems". | Only large features are priced; the small ones — the actual killer — pass unexamined. | OpenTTD feature-request policy; project logic |
| 7 | "each is days of work, and each keeps charging after release" | Connects the estimate to the ongoing cost, in plain numbers. | The estimate stops at implementation; the second and third costs are invisible. | OpenMW; Homebrew acceptance criteria |
| 8 | Three upkeep examples: bug fixed in three places, save format to migrate, a test updated twice | Makes "upkeep" concrete and checkable instead of an abstraction. | "Maintenance cost" becomes a phrase nobody can act on; estimates stay optimistic in the same way every time. | OpenMW "maintaining features comes at a cost" |
| 9 | "Nothing is refused here for lack of ambition. It is refused for lack of room." | Separates the value judgment from the capacity judgment, so a cut is not an insult to the idea. | A cut reads as "the idea is bad"; the developer argues about quality instead of capacity and the budget loses. | Homebrew: criteria "does not guarantee acceptance"; OpenTTD "we really appreciate feedback and ideas" |
| 10 | Budget contents: features, content in numbers, cut list | The three things a stage budget must state; each answers a different question (what, how much, what goes first). | A budget with features only cannot be checked; one with numbers only has no priority order when time runs short. | Blueprint G2; k8s release cycle; TypeScript milestones |
| 11 | The number list: levels, items, enemies, words, minutes | Forces the budget into countable units and covers both content-heavy and time-based games. | "Content" stays uncountable; the gate argues about scope in adjectives. | Blueprint G2; R1 "count read from the running build" |
| 12 | Cut list defined as "what leaves first if the stage runs long" | A budget needs a pre-agreed order of retreat, decided while calm. | Cuts are made in a panic at the deadline, and the first thing cut is the thing that made the game interesting. | raylib `_DISCARDED_` entries with reasons; OpenTTD strict policy |
| 13 | "It sits in `STATE.md`, copied from the gate that set it" | Gives the budget one home and one origin, so the number cannot be re-invented mid-stage. | Two budgets exist (the gate's and the memory's); the developer quotes whichever is convenient. | Blueprint D02 (gate state); R5 "one fact in one place" |
| 14 | "Over budget means cut or park. It never means expand." | The decision procedure when the number is exceeded: two moves, not a third. | The default response to a full budget becomes "extend the stage"; the budget stops binding after its first breach. | TypeScript: issues outside the milestone do not accept PRs; k8s freeze |
| 15 | "Moving a line off the cut list is the same act as adding a feature" | Closes the loophole: cuts are reversible only through the same accounting as additions. | The cut list becomes a parking lot that quietly re-enters; the budget is exceeded with paperwork that looks compliant. | TypeScript milestone rule; k8s Exception Request |
| 16 | New idea: one line with what, value, cost | Sets the minimum record that makes a parked idea usable later: identity, reason, price. | The backlog fills with one-word entries nobody can price or decide; it stops being read. | Blueprint D05; Homebrew acceptance criteria; OpenTTD feature requests |
| 17 | "Then it waits." | States that recording is the complete action; nothing else happens now. | Writing the entry is treated as the first step of building it; the stage absorbs the idea by increments. | godot: proposals live outside the issue tracker; OpenMW `Future` label |
| 18 | "Nothing is rejected — the backlog is where a good idea keeps its value until a gate can pay for it" | Explains why parking is not losing, so the developer records instead of arguing. | Ideas are argued in the moment (because "no" feels final) or dropped silently and re-derived later at full cost. | Homebrew third-party tap; OpenMW `Future`; OpenTTD one-year closure (rejected: closure) |
| 19 | "Writing the line takes a minute. Building the idea takes the stage." | A ratio the developer can feel at the moment of temptation. | The entry looks like overhead equal to the work; it is skipped and the idea is built. | OpenTTD "please do ask first"; project logic |
| 20 | G2 sets the content budget in numbers, "from what the slice proved" | Ties the number to evidence rather than optimism, and names the gate that owns it. | The budget is set by ambition; G2 becomes a demo review with no commitment to what follows. | Blueprint G2; R1 evidence; k8s Enhancements Freeze |
| 21 | G2.5 freezes features; "content and polish only: no new mechanic, system, or mode" | Defines the freeze by what it excludes, with three nouns that cover the usual exceptions. | Every freeze has an exception ("it's small", "it's content"); the phase after G2.5 becomes another feature phase. | Blueprint G2.5; k8s Enhancements Freeze and Code Freeze |
| 22 | One in, one out, "a feature of comparable cost, named in the same decision" | Makes the exception expensive and visible; "comparable cost" blocks trading a mode for a label. | Additions after freeze are free; the freeze holds on paper and leaks in practice. | R6 one-in-one-out; k8s Exception Request (rejected: the paperwork) |
| 23 | "R7 applies the same trade to the library" | Points at the existing mechanism instead of duplicating it. | A second, subtly different one-in-one-out rule exists in core; the two drift. | R6; rubric "one fact in one place" |
| 24 | "A fix that restores intended behavior is not a feature; a fix that changes a system is." | Gives the freeze a test for the most common exception claim, so "it's a fix" has an answer that is not negotiation. | Any change can be relabeled a fix; the freeze holds for named features and leaks through everything else. | Blueprint G2.5; R6 "add only after failure" |
| 25 | "R7's tinker budget ... is not product scope; R7 owns it" | Excludes exploration from the budget, so the rule cannot be used to close the only free space. | R9 is applied to tinkering and kills the divergence the framework depends on; or R7 and R9 contradict at the boundary. | R7 tinker budget |
| 26 | "R9 prices what enters the product, never what you try in private" | States the boundary positively, so both rules can be applied without negotiation. | The boundary is re-argued every time; one of the two rules is ignored depending on who is tired. | R7; OpenTTD fork discussion (rejected: forks as the only outlet) |
| 27 | S10 builds the slice; S11 owns the cut list, its order, and the reuse matrix | Routes the procedure to the skills that hold it and refuses to restate it — including the order, which decides what leaves first. | R9 grows into a second content procedure that disagrees with S11 on the cut order; or the order is nobody's and the cut list is unordered when it is needed. | Blueprint S10, S11 |
| 28 | "Scope questions go through R2 and its question budget, not into a debate" | Keeps scope from becoming an unbounded interview, without restating R2's number (a restated number would drift). | Each scope dispute is argued at length until the budget is forgotten, and R2's budget is bypassed through the scope door. | R2 |
| 29 | Check: E06 — idea lands in BACKLOG, written scope unchanged | One observable outcome, scored by an existing eval. | "The budget was respected" is unfalsifiable; A04 has nothing to read. | Blueprint E06 |
| 30 | A04 reads `STATE.md` against `BACKLOG.md`; fails scope that grew without a cut | Names the reviewer and the two files, so the check is a diff, not an opinion. | The review judges intent; a stage that grew by ten small features passes because each was reasonable. | Blueprint A04, E06 |
| 31 | "At G2 and G2.5 the budget is the numbers written in the gate record" | Binds the check to the gate's one-line-plus-date format instead of a new artifact. | The gate decision is prose; nobody can tell later which numbers were agreed. | Blueprint gates ("one line plus a date"), D02 |

## Deliberate omissions

| Omitted | Reason |
|---|---|
| A sprint plan, task list, or story format | R9 states the budget and the gate points; planning belongs to the partner agent and S10. A plan here would be stale within a week. |
| A numeric cap for content (how many levels a game needs) | That number is project-specific; the rule requires a number, it cannot supply one. |
| The cut order method (cost, risk, fun) | S11 owns the cut list; a method here would compete with it. |
| A reuse matrix or content pipeline | S11 owns both; restating them creates two sources of truth. |
| A backlog file format beyond one line | D05 owns the document; R9 only requires value and cost in the line. |
| A definition of "feature" vs "content" | The gate record decides per project; a taxonomy invites the argument it is meant to end. |
| Exceptions after freeze beyond one-in-one-out | Every extra exception path is a door the freeze cannot close. |
| Time-boxing the backlog review | Review cadence belongs to the gate and the partner agent, not to a rule. |
| A rule for pricing an idea in hours | Solo estimates in hours are fiction; the rule asks for a cost, not a precision. |
| Engine, OS, or tooling specifics | Core rules must stay portable; no engine imports or tool names. |
| A new eval ID | The blueprint assigns E06 to this rule; a second check would split the score. |
| Advice on saying no to a stakeholder | R2 owns dialogue; R9 owns accounting. |
